stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Cities often use height limits to keep sunlight on narrow streets. Under a new zoning plan, the downtown is divided into five districts, each with its own rules. The height limit for buildings in all five districts ______ set by the city's planning board, which reviews it every ten years.
explanation: Cross out the prepositional phrases "for buildings" and "in all five districts." That leaves "The height limit ______ set." The subject is "limit," which is singular, so it takes "is." This is the basic move behind every SAT agreement question that puts a long phrase between the subject and the verb: remove the phrase, then match the verb to the noun that is left.

A.why: You matched the verb to "districts," the plural noun right before the blank. "Districts" is inside the phrase "in all five districts," so it can't be the subject. The subject is "limit," which is singular.

C.why: "Being" is not a main verb. With it, the sentence has a subject, "limit," but no verb, so it isn't a complete sentence. The blank needs a conjugated verb such as "is."

D.why: "To be" is an infinitive, and an infinitive can't be a sentence's main verb. "The height limit to be set by the board" is a fragment. You need a conjugated verb that agrees with "limit."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Carbon composites are prized in aircraft design because they are both light and stiff. The thin fibers inside a single sheet of the finished panel ______ laid at right angles to one another, an arrangement that spreads a load evenly across the sheet.
explanation: Cross out "inside a single sheet" and "of the finished panel." That leaves "The thin fibers ______ laid." The subject is "fibers," which is plural, so it takes "are." On the real test, the clutter often ends in a singular noun placed in front of a plural subject, just as it does here.

A.why: You matched the verb to "panel" or "sheet," the singular nouns right before the blank. Both are inside prepositional phrases. The noun doing the verb is "fibers," which is plural.

B.why: "Being" can't act as a main verb. With it, "fibers" never gets a verb, and the sentence is a fragment.

D.why: "To be" is an infinitive, not a conjugated verb. The sentence needs a main verb that agrees with "fibers," and an infinitive can't fill that role.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Scholars who study a composer's working habits often begin with the handwritten scores. For one little-known nineteenth-century composer, the only surviving manuscript of her three string quartets ______ kept in a small city library, where researchers can examine it by appointment.
explanation: Cross out "of her three string quartets." That leaves "the only surviving manuscript ______ kept." The subject is "manuscript," which is singular, so it takes "is." When an SAT question puts an "of" phrase with a plural noun between the subject and the verb, this check is the whole question.

B.why: You matched the verb to "quartets," the plural noun right before the blank. "Quartets" is the object of "of," so it isn't the subject. There is one manuscript, so the verb must be singular.

C.why: "To be" is an infinitive, so it can't be the main verb. With it, the sentence has the subject "manuscript" but no verb that completes it.

D.why: "Being" is an -ing form, and it can't work as a main verb by itself. "The manuscript being kept in a library" is a fragment, not a sentence.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When wolves returned to one mountain valley, ecologists tracked the effects for more than a decade. The wolves that rangers released into the valley ______ changed where the elk graze, and the willows along the river have grown back as a result.
explanation: Cross out the clause "that rangers released into the valley." That leaves "The wolves ______ changed." The subject is "wolves," which is plural, so it takes "have." SAT questions often put a "that" or "which" clause between the subject and the verb. You can always lift that clause out to find the subject.

A.why: You matched the verb to "valley," the singular noun right before the blank. "Valley" belongs to the "that" clause. The animals that changed the elk's grazing are the wolves, so the verb must be plural.

B.why: "Having" is an -ing form, not a main verb. With it, the main clause has the subject "wolves" but no verb, so it is a fragment.

C.why: "To have" is an infinitive, and an infinitive can't be the main verb for "wolves." The sentence needs a conjugated verb that agrees with a plural subject.
